source.title: Neural network optimization strategies and the topography of the loss landscape

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including supplementary material.
record.tranche_reason: Compares SGD with L-BFGS-GSS and measures training/test loss and landscape properties in four MNIST networks; it tests optimizer-related generalization using a different optimization method and measures.
record.gate_note: The optimizer comparison and training/test losses are direct results for V4. Path heights, weight distributions, and kPCA are results about landscape structure, but do not measure the specific properties named in V7. No results test the other versions. Claims about prior studies in the introduction and discussion are not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study compares SGD with a deterministic quasi-Newton optimizer, not the adaptive gradient methods named in V4. Its landscape measurements do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or its association with generalization gaps. Although Table I includes convolutional and fully connected classifiers, it reports cross-entropy loss rather than V3's classification error. None of the eight versions is directly tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' interpretation: SGD finds more compact, connected, generalizable solution regions, whereas L-BFGS-GSS can reach deeper, more isolated and overfit solutions. Add that early stopping gives similar test performance and the autoencoder is an exception. Flatness and curvature are interpretations of the landscape analyses, not measurements of V7's magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SGD versus customized full-batch L-BFGS-GSS with Golden Section Search; trains on MNIST, selects 48 of 75 initializations, and uses early stopping at minimum test loss for the test-weight sets. Not an adaptive-optimizer comparison of the kind in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer choice changes training/test losses, path barriers, weight spread, and kPCA separation. Autoencoder differs from the three classification architectures in test-loss comparison and barrier behavior. For test-weight kPCA, separation nearly disappears for FCP and LeNet but persists for Autoencoder and LSTM; the training-weight separation appears with RBF kPCA and disappears with other kernels and standard PCA.

fits_no_version.finding: L-BFGS-GSS reaches lower training loss in all four architectures. Minimum test losses are numerically higher than SGD's for the three classifiers but lower for the autoencoder; the authors describe test performance with early stopping as comparable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quasi-Newton and stochastic gradient optimization can differ strongly in fitting while having similar early-stopped classification losses.

fits_no_version.finding: LeNet has lower test cross-entropy than FCP under both optimizers: 0.0417 versus 0.0969 for L-BFGS-GSS and 0.0389 versus 0.0825 for SGD. Classification-error rates are not reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LeNet achieves lower minimum MNIST test cross-entropy than this fully connected perceptron.

fits_no_version.finding: SGD solutions have lower connecting-path heights for FCP, LeNet, and LSTM on training and test landscapes; the autoencoder is an exception.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer choice affects connectivity between independently trained solutions.

fits_no_version.finding: L-BFGS-GSS has larger weight-component standard deviations. RBF kPCA separates BFGS training weights from SGD test weights; using test weights for both removes most separation for FCP and LeNet but not Autoencoder and LSTM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer and checkpoint selection affect parameter spread and kernel-dependent separation.

record.problems: Only MNIST is studied; no uncertainty estimates are reported for averages or path distributions. The authors select the 48 lowest-training-loss solutions from 75 initializations. The adaptive-optimizer claim is only indirectly addressed because L-BFGS-GSS is not an adaptive gradient method. Test loss is used to select early-stopped weights.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and chance-level held-out performance versus natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected classification error, local connectivity, sparse connections, and transferred initialization.
All adaptive-gradient comparisons and the stated tuning, weight-decay, switching, and language-model qualifications.
Batch-size interventions under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations; optimizer and batching differ together here.
Dropout interventions and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm and margin measures.

record.verdict_notes: All states are cannot_determine relative to the claim versions, not denials of the reported structural differences. Training and test losses in Table I use different checkpoints, so their subtraction would not give a same-model generalization gap. Test data are used for checkpoint selection, and averages cover 48 runs selected for low training loss from 75 initializations.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
CNN versus fully connected test error and architectural bias.
Adaptive optimizers, broader hyperparameter tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching optimizers, and language benchmarks.
Large batch sizes, fixed epoch budgets, and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: FCP, LeNet CNN, and LSTM on MNIST, L-BFGS-GSS versus SGD with early stopping
reader_labels.reason: L-BFGS-GSS has lower training loss but higher test loss than SGD in these three architectures (R1–R4, R7–R8), consistent with worse held-out performance despite stronger fitting.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The L-BFGS-GSS autoencoder has both lower training and lower test loss than SGD (R5–R6), reversing the classifier pattern; this is an unsupervised reconstruction task.
